sentences.text: Ultrastenos was a small crocodilian measuring upwards of 1.5 meters in length, possessing a flattened and short snout contrary to earlier proposals that it was elongated.

Its external nostrils were positioned very close to the tip of the snout, giving the premaxilla a steep profile, while the nostrils themselves were longer than wide and opened slightly forward rather than straight up. The nasal bones extended across the snout and touched the nostrils.
The supratemporal openings in the skull were prominent and teardrop-shaped.
The genus was described in 2016 based on a holotype specimen found at the Low Lion Site of the Riversleigh World Heritage Area, though fossils are also known from the White Hunter Site.

Ultrastenos is believed to have been a semi-aquatic generalist with a broad, platyrostral skull, similar to Baru wickeni. During the Late Oligocene, the Low Lion Site was covered by open forests lacking extensive river systems or wetlands. The animal likely inhabited forest lakes and ponds drained by karstic limestone.

The type species was originally designated as Ultrastenos willisi, while Ultrastenos huberi was initially described as a subdivision of the genus. Due to priority rules, the valid species name is now Ultrastenos huberi, honoring Professor Huber.

Stein et al. (2016) classified Ultrastenos as a mekosuchine crocodilian and a sister taxon to Trilophosuchus rackhami. Rio and Mannion published a study in 2021 discussing the phylogenetic position of Ultrastenos, while Lee and Yates (2018) recovered "Baru" huberi as closely related to the Bullock Creek taxon.
Ultrastenos lived during the Chattian stage, from 27.3 to 23.04 million years ago.

It is debated whether Ultrastenos had a slender snout, as later studies suggest the initial interpretation of a narrow mandible was a misinterpretation and the animal actually had a more generalized lower jaw. Researchers suggested that a re-description of the taxon was necessary following the discovery of related forms. Willis previously considered Ultrastenos and Baru to be the same genus, using skull features to distinguish between them. There is a disagreement regarding the number of premaxillary teeth in juvenile Ultrastenos, with older claims of five teeth based on a specimen now classified as Baru wickeni contrasting with newer findings. Research suggests that the fossils of Ultrastenos and the previously named species Baru huberi belong to the same animal. It is debated whether certain cranial fossils belong to Ultrastenos or to the species Baru wickeni, with some researchers proposing they belong to a juvenile Baru wickeni.
